summary: German has two everyday negators. kein (declined like ein, with a plural keine) negates a noun that would otherwise have ein or no article: ein Apfel → kein Apfel, Wasser → kein Wasser, Äpfel → keine Äpfel; as an object, the masculine is keinen (Ich trinke keinen Kaffee). nicht negates everything else: verbs, adjectives, places, and nouns with der/die/das, dieser or a possessive (Ich mag den Käse nicht. Das ist nicht mein Bruder.). In a simple sentence nicht stands at the end, after the object (Ich esse den Fisch nicht), but before an adjective, a place or a second verb (nicht gut, nicht hier, nicht kochen). The other negative words replace both: nichts (nothing), niemand (nobody; object niemanden), nie / niemals (never) and weder … noch (neither … nor). Standard German allows only ONE negation per clause: Ich esse nichts – never *Ich esse nicht nichts: a negative word is the whole negation. The answer word is nein; “yes” to a negative question is doch (S09).

blocks.title: Only one negation
blocks.text: Ich esse nichts. Niemand kocht. Ich trinke nie Kaffee. – No nicht or kein beside them: one negative word per clause is enough.

blocks.title: nein is an answer, not a negator
blocks.text: Nein, danke. Ich will keinen Tee. – nein answers a question; inside the sentence you need nicht or kein.

askYourself: Am I negating a noun with ein or with no article? → kein (with the ending of ein; masculine object keinen).
Otherwise (verb, adjective, place, noun with der/die/das or mein) → nicht.
Where does nicht go? At the end after the object – but before an adjective, a place or an infinitive.
Do I mean nothing / nobody / never / neither … nor? → nichts, niemand, nie, weder … noch – and no other negation.
Is it an answer? nein = no; doch = yes after a negative question.
steps: Choose kein, nicht or a negative word.
Give kein its ending; place nicht.

traps: *Ich habe nicht ein Brot is not the normal negation → Ich habe kein Brot.
kein has a plural: keine Äpfel (ein has none).
Masculine object: Ich trinke keinen Kaffee, not *kein Kaffee.
Both are possible for a general dislike: Ich mag keinen Käse = Ich mag Käse nicht (kein is more usual).
No double negation: Ich esse nichts, not *Ich esse nicht nichts.
nein is only an answer word: Ich mag keine Zwiebeln, not *Ich mag nein Zwiebeln.
weder … noch already negates: Ich habe weder Brot noch Käse (no kein).

quiz.why: Kaffee without an article → kein; der Kaffee is masculine and an object → keinen.
A noun with der/die/das is negated with nicht, at the end.
The verb stays second; nicht goes before the place word; kein never negates a place.
niemand as an object: niemanden (spoken also niemand).

seeAlso.note: Arabic chooses the negator by tense: لَا lā (present), لَمْ lam (past), لَنْ lan (future), لَيْسَ laysa (“is not”), مَا mā.
Hebrew לֹא before the verb, אֵין for “there is no / not have”: אֵין לִי לֶחֶם (I have no bread).
Chinese 不 for the present and habits, 没 for the past and with 有: 我不喝咖啡, 我没有面包.
doch – the “yes” that contradicts a negative question (S09).

notes.text: Greek needs δεν with τίποτα (δεν τρώω τίποτα); German has one negation: Ich esse nichts. δεν stands before the verb; nicht usually goes late (Ich esse den Fisch nicht). δεν έχω ψωμί is Ich habe kein Brot.
Russian doubles the negation (я ничего не ем) and puts не before the verb; German says Ich esse nichts, with nicht late in the clause. у меня нет хлеба is Ich habe kein Brot.
Spanish needs no with nada (no como nada); German has one negation: Ich esse nichts.
“no” before a noun is kein (no bread – kein Brot), and standard English also has one negation (I eat nothing). But German has no do: Ich esse nicht, and nein is only the answer word.
ne … pas surrounds the verb; German has one word, late in the clause (Ich esse den Fisch nicht). pas de pain is kein Brot, ne … rien is nichts.
nahī̃ stands before the verb (maĩ nahī̃ khātā); German nicht goes late in the clause, and a noun with ein or no article takes kein.
Persian negates with the prefix na- / ne- on the verb (nemixoram); German uses separate words, nicht or kein.
Marathi puts nāhī after the verb (mī khāt nāhī), which is close to German nicht at the end (Ich esse nicht); a noun with ein or no article takes kein instead.
Arabic changes the negator with the tense and type of sentence (lā, lam, lan, laysa); German uses nicht and kein in every tense.
Hebrew doubles the negation (af echad lo ba, “nobody not came”) and says ein li for “I have no”; German has one negation (Niemand kommt) and Ich habe kein …

Turkish negates inside the verb (yemiyorum), uses değil for nouns and yok for absence (ekmeğim yok); German uses separate words: nicht, kein (Ich habe kein Brot). hiç kimse still needs the negative verb (hiç kimse gelmedi); German niemand stands alone: Niemand kommt.
Japanese negates with a verb ending (tabenai, tabemasen); German uses separate words, nicht and kein.
Korean puts an before the verb or adds -ji anta; German has nicht late in the clause and kein for nouns.
Finnish negates with a verb that takes the person (en, et, ei … syö); German nicht never changes and kein changes like ein.
Hungarian doubles the negation (nem eszem semmit, senki sem jött); German uses one negative word: Ich esse nichts. Niemand kommt.
Swahili negates with prefixes and a changed verb form (ninakula → sili); German leaves the verb as it is and adds nicht or kein.
不 and 没 stand before the verb (我不吃 / 我没有面包); German has nicht late in the clause and kein for nouns: Ich esse nicht. Ich habe kein Brot.
không stands before the verb (tôi không ăn); German nicht usually comes later (Ich esse das nicht), and kein negates a noun.
Inuktitut negates with a suffix inside the verb (-nngit-); German uses separate words: nicht, kein, nichts.
